rows.stem: Three numbers in AP have the sum 30. What is its middle term ?
rows.solution:
Let the three numbers be \(a - d\), \(a\) and \(a + d\), where a is the middle term.

Their sum is \(3a = 30\), so \(a = 10\). This is option (B) 10.

rows.stem: An arc of a circle is of length \(5\pi\) cm and the sector it bounds has an area of \(20\pi\,\text{cm}^2\). Its radius is :
rows.solution:
The area of a sector is half the product of its arc length and the radius: \(\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} l r\).

\(20\pi = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5\pi \times r\), so \(r = \dfrac{40\pi}{5\pi} = 8\) cm. This is option (D) 8 cm.

rows.stem: If \(\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ\) and \(\alpha = 2\beta\), then \(\cos^2\alpha + \sin^2\beta\) is equal to :
rows.solution:
From \(\alpha = 2\beta\) and \(\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ\): \(3\beta = 90^\circ\), so \(\beta = 30^\circ\) and \(\alpha = 60^\circ\).

\(\cos^2 60^\circ + \sin^2 30^\circ = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), which is option (B) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).

rows.stem: If the length of a chord of a circle is equal to its radius, then the angle subtended by chord at the centre is :
rows.solution:
Let the chord be AB in a circle with centre O. Then \(OA = OB\) (radii) and \(AB = OA\) (given), so triangle OAB is equilateral.

Every angle of an equilateral triangle is \(60^\circ\), so \(\angle AOB = 60^\circ\), which is option (A) \(60^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: The greatest number which divides 70 and 125, leaving remainders 5 and 8 respectively, is :
rows.solution:
The required number divides \(70 - 5 = 65\) and \(125 - 8 = 117\) exactly, so it is their HCF.

\(65 = 5 \times 13\) and \(117 = 3^2 \times 13\), so the HCF is 13 (which is larger than both remainders, as a divisor must be). This is option (A) 13.

rows.stem: A ladder 14 m long leans against a wall. If the foot of the ladder is 7 m from the wall, then the angle of elevation of the top of the wall is :
rows.solution:
The ladder is the hypotenuse (14 m) and the distance of its foot from the wall is the base (7 m). If \(\theta\) is the angle the ladder makes with the ground,

\(\cos\theta = \dfrac{7}{14} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(\theta = 60^\circ\). This is option (D) \(60^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: If the zeroes of the polynomial \(x^2 + ax + b\) are in the ratio \(3 : 4\), then prove that \(12a^2 = 49b\).
rows.solution:
Since the zeroes are in the ratio \(3 : 4\), let them be \(3\alpha\) and \(4\alpha\).

Sum of zeroes: \(3\alpha + 4\alpha = -a\), so \(7\alpha = -a\).

Product of zeroes: \(3\alpha \times 4\alpha = b\), so \(12\alpha^2 = b\).

Then \(12a^2 = 12(-7\alpha)^2 = 49 \times 12\alpha^2 = 49b\), as required.

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: If the radii of the bases of a cylinder and a cone are in the ratio \(3 : 4\) and their heights are in the ratio \(2 : 3\), find the ratio of their volumes.
rows.solution:
Let the cylinder have radius \(r_1\) and height \(h_1\), and the cone radius \(r_2\) and height \(h_2\). We are given \(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \dfrac{3}{4}\) and \(\dfrac{h_1}{h_2} = \dfrac{2}{3}\).

\(\dfrac{\text{Volume of cylinder}}{\text{Volume of cone}} = \dfrac{\pi r_1^2 h_1}{\frac{1}{3}\pi r_2^2 h_2} = 3 \times \left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^2 \times \dfrac{h_1}{h_2}\)

\(= 3 \times \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 3 \times \dfrac{9}{16} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{9}{8}\)

So the ratio of the volumes of the cylinder and the cone is \(9 : 8\).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: Three sets of Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics books have to be stacked in such a way that all the books are stored subject-wise and the height of each stack is the same. The number of Physics books is 144, the number of Chemistry books is 180 and the number of Mathematics books is 192. Assuming that the books are of same thickness, determine the number of stacks of Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics books.
rows.solution:
Each stack must have the same height and the books all have the same thickness, so every stack holds the same number of books. That number must divide 144, 180 and 192, and to use the fewest stacks it should be the largest such number, the HCF.

\(144 = 2^4 \times 3^2\), \(180 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5\), \(192 = 2^6 \times 3\).

HCF \(= 2^2 \times 3 = 12\), so each stack has 12 books.

Number of stacks of Physics books \(= \dfrac{144}{12} = 12\), of Chemistry books \(= \dfrac{180}{12} = 15\), and of Mathematics books \(= \dfrac{192}{12} = 16\).

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: A two-digit number is such that the product of its digits is 12. When 36 is added to this number, the digits interchange their places. Find the number.
rows.solution:
Let the tens digit be x and the units digit be y, so the number is \(10x + y\).

Product of the digits: \(xy = 12\) ... (i)

Adding 36 reverses the digits: \(10x + y + 36 = 10y + x\), so \(9x - 9y + 36 = 0\), that is \(y = x + 4\) ... (ii)

Substituting (ii) in (i): \(x(x + 4) = 12\), so \(x^2 + 4x - 12 = 0\).

\((x + 6)(x - 2) = 0\), so \(x = 2\) (a digit cannot be negative) and \(y = 6\).

The number is 26. Check: \(2 \times 6 = 12\) and \(26 + 36 = 62\).

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: A student scored a total of 32 marks in class tests in Mathematics and Science. Had he scored 2 marks less in Science and 4 marks more in Mathematics, the product of his marks would have been 253. Find his marks in the two subjects.
rows.solution:
Let his marks be x in Mathematics and y in Science.

Total: \(x + y = 32\), so \(y = 32 - x\) ... (i)

With 4 more in Mathematics and 2 less in Science: \((x + 4)(y - 2) = 253\) ... (ii)

Substituting (i) in (ii): \((x + 4)(30 - x) = 253\), so \(-x^2 + 26x + 120 = 253\), that is \(x^2 - 26x + 133 = 0\).

\((x - 19)(x - 7) = 0\), so \(x = 19\) or \(x = 7\).

If \(x = 19\), then \(y = 13\); if \(x = 7\), then \(y = 25\). Both satisfy the conditions: \(23 \times 11 = 253\) and \(11 \times 23 = 253\).

So his marks in Mathematics and Science are 19 and 13, or 7 and 25.
